extracted.intended_audience: general literate public / readers of The Spectator (early 18th-century) interested in manners, conduct, and moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Short, conversational moral and social essays in the Spectator tradition offering prescriptive reflections on conduct, cheerfulness, friendship, and agreeable behaviour. These pieces mix anecdote, character sketches, and practical maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour about oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat candour about one's own faults as a virtue: 'let us at this time behold only the natural Consequence of Candour when we speak of ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge faults rather than persisting in false pretences; public confession of one's faults can win sympathy and relieve shame (example: the criminal who, by confessing, turned pity from conviction). Anti-pattern: obstinacy in the wrong out of vanity or a mistaken idea of 'high spirit'—this is the conduct of 'little Minds' and leads to guilt, sorrow, and perplexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of spirit = acknowledging error
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a diminution of greatness of spirit to have been in the wrong; 'Perfection is not the Attribute of Man, therefore he is not degraded by the Acknowledgment of an Imperfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate firmness with persisting in error; true greatness allows correction and discarding of faults. Anti-pattern: imitating fortitude by stubbornly defending faults, even those of one's servants or allies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities essential to Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is 'a strong and habitual Inclination in two Persons to promote the Good and Happiness of one another.' Love and esteem are the first principles; envy and inconstancy are incompatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship requires both affection and respect—one can love without esteem and esteem without love, but true friendship needs both. It neutralizes envy; similarity of temperament is not required and may be less important than fidelity and steady support (examples: Achates, Atticus). Prefer a prudent, steady friend to an ostentatiously zealous one.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to reproach or correct a friend
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproaches from a friend 'should always be strictly just, and not too frequent.' The aim is the friend's advantage, not self-pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give criticisms sparingly and with fairness; arrange the manner so the friend perceives advice is for his benefit. Anti-patterns: frequent or unjust reproaches that alienate the friend or destroy the desire to please; reproaches that humiliate rather than help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of duties to friends
rubrics_metrics.description: We are 'in some measure more inexcusable if we violate our Duties to a Friend, than to a Relation' because friendship is a voluntary choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat obligations to friends seriously—friendship arises from choice and thus carries a moral weight that deserves fidelity and careful behavior (implication: don't betray or abandon a friend lightly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of being agreeable in company
rubrics_metrics.description: The true art of being agreeable is 'to appear well pleased with those you are engaged with, and rather to seem well entertained, than to bring Entertainment to others.' Natural disposition, good sense, good nature, and discretion make one universally welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt naturally to the tone of the company (not by artifice); show genuine pleasure in others and avoid dominating or deriding them. Anti-patterns: attempting artificial variability to please every audience, forcing oneself into company when inclined to be solitary, being the 'messenger' who only recounts his own recent experiences, and witty persons who deride or ungracefully distinguish others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness over artifice in social behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviour that springs from nature and disposition is preferable to artful performance; 'there can be no such thing as Art in it' if it is merely assumed to gain praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine temper and manners rather than studied parts. While many conversational skills can be learned, true facility (facetiæ) that delights without affectation is an innate quality. Anti-pattern: putting on an artful part merely to win praise—this is despicable prostitution of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness as a habitual good (health and mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness 'is, in the first place, the best Promoter of Health' and preserves the mind by banishing anxious care and composing the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cheerfulness as a habit: attend to nature and pleasurable objects (sun, green landscapes, birdsong) which sustain cheerfulness; recognize the mutual relation of health and cheerfulness (many who 'wear well' have gaiety). Examples and quasi-scientific explanation: certain colours (green) and natural scenes soothe the eye and spirit. Anti-pattern: repining and secret murmurs that wear out the vital frame and disturb the animal spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence and honouring the wounded/veterans
rubrics_metrics.description: Act of employing or honouring those wounded in service as a sign of gratitude and humanity: e.g., Sir Roger 'never make[s] use of any body to row me, that has not either lost a Leg or an Arm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferentially employ or show special regard to those who have served and been wounded; treat such acts as both moral duty and social honour. Anti-pattern: indifferent or contemptuous treatment of veterans and the wounded.
